The central argument is that vanity-based goals are often more motivating than general health goals because progress is visible, frequently evaluated, and socially reinforced. Many of the behaviors used to improve physical appearance—such as exercising, improving nutrition, and losing weight—also provide meaningful health benefits. Consequently, pursuing an appearance-related goal may indirectly produce better health outcomes than pursuing health as a broad goal in itself.

Vanity goals may also feel more immediately valuable because they can influence socially significant outcomes, such as attracting a partner and receiving the benefits associated with society’s preference for physically attractive people. General health goals, by comparison, are often connected to abstract and delayed outcomes, including longevity and long-term well-being. Because the rewards of vanity goals are more immediate and observable, they may generate stronger motivation and faster progress.
